'''Frances Evelyn Cave-Browne-Cave''' [[Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society|FRAS]] (1876–1965) was an English [[mathematician]] and educator.

==Early life==
Frances Cave-Browne-Cave was the daughter of Sir Thomas Cave-Browne-Cave and Blanche Matilda Mary Ann Milton. She was educated at home in [[Streatham Common]] with her sisters and entered [[Girton College]], [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]], with her elder sister [[Beatrice Mabel Cave-Browne-Cave]] in 1895. She obtained a first-class degree and she would have been Fifth [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]] in 1898 if she had been a man. She took Part II of the [[Mathematical Tripos]] in 1899.<ref name= "ODNB">{{Cite ODNB|id= 61586 |title=Cave, (Frances) Evelyn Cave-Browne- (1876–1965), mathematician |last=Davis |first=A.E.L.}}</ref>

==Career and continued studies==
Like her sister, she was usually known by the single surname Cave professionally.<ref name= "ODNB"/> Along with Beatrice, she worked with [[Karl Pearson]] at [[University College London]].<ref>David Alan Grier, ''When Computers Were Human'', Princeton University Press, 2005, pp. 111–112</ref> Her work was funded by the first research grant offered at Girton: an Old Students' Research Studentship from Girton, provided by [[Florence Margaret Durham]].<ref name= "WiM">{{cite book |last1=Beery |first1=Janet L. |last2=Greenwald |first2=Sarah J. |last3=Jensen-Vallin |first3=Jacqueline A. |last4=Mast |first4=Maura B. |title=Women in Mathematics: Celebrating the Centennial of the Mathematical Association of America |date=2017 |publisher=Springer |isbn=9783319666945 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eDVBDwAAQBAJ&q=evelyn+cave+browne+cave&pg=PA20 |language=en}}</ref> She also received a stipend as a result of a grant to Pearson's laboratory from the [[Worshipful Company of Drapers]].<ref>[https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Cave-Browne-Cave_Evelyn/ Frances Evelyn Cave-Browne-Cave], mathshistory, St Andrews</ref> Her research in the field of [[meteorology]] produced two publications in the ''[[Proceedings of the Royal Society]]'' which discussed [[Barometer|barometric measurements]], and was read to the British Association at Cambridge in 1904.<ref name="WiM" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite news|title=Miss F. E. Cave-Browne-Cave|date=2 April 1965|work=The Times|issue=56286|page=18}}</ref>

In 1903, Cave returned to Girton as a fellow. She prioritised teaching over research, and focused on developing the weakest students because she felt that was where the biggest difference could be made.<ref name="ODNB" /> She became the director of studies in 1918.<ref name="WiM" /> She was on the executive council of the college and was largely responsible for drafting the charter of incorporation granted in 1924.<ref name=":0" /> On the 11 November 1921 she was elected a [[Royal Astronomical Society|Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title=1921MNRAS..82....1. Page 1|journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|year=1921 |volume=82 |page=1 |doi=10.1093/mnras/82.1.1 |bibcode=1921MNRAS..82....1.|doi-access=free}}</ref> Cave was made honorary fellow of Girton in 1942.<ref name="WiM" />

Cave received an MA from [[Trinity College, Dublin]]  in 1907 as a [[steamboat ladies|steamboat lady]]<ref>[https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Cave-Browne-Cave_Evelyn/ Frances Evelyn Cave-Browne-Cave], mathshistory, St Andrews</ref> since the rules of Cambridge University did not then permit women to take degrees, and from Cambridge in 1926.<ref name="WiM" />

==Later life and death==
Cave retired to Southampton in 1936. She died in [[Shedfield]] in a nursing home on 30 March 1965.<ref name= "ODNB"/>
